analysis.one_liner: Requires federal dams to deliver maximum possible water to California farm and city water contractors during droughts.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its water subcommittee, and never received a committee vote or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill tells the Interior and Commerce Departments to run California's federal Central Valley Project and let the State Water Project deliver as much water as legally possible to their contractors — largely farm water districts, plus cities and wildlife refuges — during drought. It relaxes pumping limits set to protect Delta smelt and salmon unless agencies can prove tighter restrictions are needed, fast-tracks approvals on 7-to-30-day timelines, and extends funding authority for new reservoir projects to 2031. It sunsets when the Governor's drought emergency ends or by fall 2023.
analysis.who_benefits: Central Valley agricultural water contractors get first claim on scarce drought water and relaxed environmental flow limits; municipal and industrial contractors, State Water Project contractors, and Central Valley wildlife refuges also get more water; new storage projects gain a decade more of federal funding authority.
analysis.who_benefits_short: California farm and urban water contractors

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Secretaries of Interior and Commerce to operate the Central Valley Project and allow the State Water Project to provide 'the maximum quantity of water supplies possible' to agricultural, municipal and industrial, and refuge contractors during the drought [S2][S3].

Relaxes Old and Middle River reverse-flow pumping limits to -5000 cfs unless agencies can show in writing that a tighter limit is necessary to avoid significant harm to a listed species, shifting the burden of proof toward more pumping [S3].

Requires final permit decisions on drought water projects within 10 days of a request, and environmental and Endangered Species Act reviews for water transfers within 30 days, sharply speeding approvals [S3].
Extends federal funding authority for federally owned and state-led storage projects to January 1, 2031, and various California water project authorizations to 2031 or 2036 [S2][S3].

Mandates meeting Level 2 and Level 4 water supply needs of Central Valley wildlife refuges through groundwater wells and purchases from willing sellers, with any resulting federal water made available to contractors [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Endangered species and the environment absorb the cost: more Delta pumping at relaxed flow limits threatens Delta smelt, salmon, and the fisheries and communities that depend on them. Faster timelines also narrow environmental review, and any additional deliveries come out of the same limited drought-year supply.
analysis.who_pays_short: Delta ecosystems, salmon runs, fishing communities

drawbacks.text: The bill mandates operations 'consistent with' the October 2019 biological opinions for smelt and salmonids — the Trump-era rules that environmental groups and the State of California challenged as inadequate — and only requires agencies to deviate toward stricter protections when they can prove it in writing, which critics saw as tilting the rules toward water deliveries [S3].
Seven-to-30-day decision deadlines compress Endangered Species Act and National Environmental Policy Act review, leaving little time to evaluate harm to fish and wildlife before water moves [S3].

The no-redirected-impacts title shields existing water users from any involuntary reduction or fiscal impact caused by the Act, meaning the costs of maximizing deliveries fall on species and unrepresented users rather than on contractors [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For drought-hit farm towns and contractors, guaranteed maximum deliveries address a real and urgent shortage, and the refuge and municipal provisions reach ordinary communities. But the bill's core trade is deliberate: more water out of the Delta means less for the fish, commercial and tribal fisheries, and Delta communities whose economies depend on salmon. The compressed timelines and burden-shifted flow limits would lock in more pumping precisely when species are most vulnerable. A bill that simply funded storage or expanded refuges would be less contested; this one resolves the water fight on one side's terms.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Natural Resources Committee, then sent to its Water, Oceans, and Wildlife subcommittee, and sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative David Valadao introduced the bill on June 17, 2021, joined by nine House Republicans including Minority Leader Kevin McCarthy, and eleven Republicans cosponsored in total [S3][S4][S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources the same day, and on July 21, 2021 to the Subcommittee on Water, Oceans, and Wildlife [S5].
No further action was taken in the House and the bill was never considered in the Senate; it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal and state agencies that operate under the current Endangered Species Act flow limits keep the existing rules unchanged, and Central Valley water contractors gain nothing beyond what existing law already provides.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced and cosponsored only by Republicans (11 Republicans, no Democrats), and it died in a committee chaired by the Democratic majority without a vote.

industries.note: The bill orders maximum drought deliveries to farm contractors and shifts flow-limit rules toward more pumping, giving agriculture first claim on scarce water. The cost falls on Delta smelt and salmon, and on fishing and Delta communities whose livelihoods depend on those fish.
City water suppliers are among the contractors entitled to maximum deliveries, so drought-year urban supplies rise alongside farm deliveries.

Relaxed Old and Middle River flow limits and faster permits mean less water for salmon runs that support West Coast fishing economies; the fishing industry's interest here runs with conservation and the public's environmental interest.
Extending funding authority for federal and state storage projects to 2031 keeps feasibility studies and potential construction work alive for another decade.
